Choose Merge, Keep or Discuss in the amber Decision column. These are proposals; the catalog and media queue are unchanged.
Clearest variations first. Clear = minor form/setup or duplicate wording. Likely = preserve a useful cue. Borderline = meaningful range, support or counting change.
Both instructions describe feet-braced seated cable rows with a still torso and a pull toward the lower torso. The elevated version adds a secured box on the seat.
Seat height and a secure support are setup details; retain the ordinary seated row movement.
Bench used only as a depth target
Both descriptions use two dumbbells held at the sides and the same squat and return. The candidate replaces the ordinary depth instruction with a light touch on the bench.
Offer a stable bench as an optional depth cue; this is not the paused seated Box Squat.
Both keep the feet planted and lower back steady while curling the shoulders a short distance. The candidate holds a plate at the chest; the base already supports optional load.
Retain optional plate loading and secure chest-level handling.
Both are overhand pull-ups from extended arms, with a controlled lowering. The candidate adds a dip-belt weight; the base already has optional load tracking.
Retain dip-belt setup and added-weight entry; do not carry over forced back arching as a requirement.
Both curl the shoulder blades a short distance from the floor with knees bent and feet planted. The candidate adds arms held overhead.
Overhead arms change leverage; offer the position as an optional form detail.
Bench/box touch as a coaching cue
The candidate says the bench teaches hip position and depth and instructs only a slight touch before standing. The base already covers the same barbell back squat.
Optional depth target and controlled touch; do not imply sitting, relaxing, or bouncing.
Crossed arms plus bench depth target
The candidate is a front squat with crossed arms and a touch of the glutes to a bench; the base has the same front-rack load and squat/stand sequence.
Comfortable front-rack grip and optional depth target can be form choices.
Both keep a bar across the front shoulders with elbows raised and squat upright. The distinguishing instruction is crossing the arms over the bar.
Cross-arm grip may be an optional secure front-rack setup.
The candidate is the same barbell back squat but requires hamstrings to reach calves. The base already permits a comfortable depth.
Depth is a range option, not a requirement to force every user below their controlled range.
Both start hanging with extended arms and pull up under control. The candidate uses a V-bar attachment for a neutral grip instead of the base overhand bar grip.
Neutral grip and a securely rated attachment are setup options; the attachment must be stable.
Both perform bilateral dumbbell curls with upper arms supported on a preacher pad. The candidate keeps the palms inward.
Neutral grip changes muscle emphasis and loading; retain the option if adopting a grip-neutral catalog.
Both put hands on a stable bench with feet back and lower the chest toward it. The candidate only specifies hands wider than shoulder width.
Keep bench stability and comfortable hand spacing in the base guidance.
Both use a straight-body floor push-up and the same elbow bend/press. The candidate specifies wide hands; the base already allows hands under or just outside the shoulders.
Retain comfortable hand-width choice as a form option.
The candidate describes only the first quarter of a sit-up, curling the torso up and down with arms crossed. That matches the base crunch; soles touching and knees apart are the added setup.
Butterfly leg position can be an optional comfort/setup cue.
Both keep the lower back on the floor and curl the shoulders up a few inches. The candidate rests the feet on a ball instead of the floor; the trunk is not on the ball.
Optional leg support and bent knees; distinguish this from Exercise Ball Crunch, which supports the torso on the ball.
Low-incline label for an existing supported reverse fly
Both lie chest down on an incline bench, keep a fixed soft elbow bend and raise dumbbells out to the sides. The candidate specifies an approximately 15-degree incline.
Comfortable support angle and unchanged rear-delt raise path.
Lying Barbell Triceps Press to Chin
Both lie on a bench and extend the elbows with the upper arms held steady. The candidate changes the lowering target from near the forehead to near the chin.
Use a comfortable path clear of the face; do not prescribe face contact.
Both use the same back-supported hack-squat machine, shoulder pads, knee/hip bend and return. The variant specifies feet about three inches apart instead of shoulder width.
Offer a comfortable stance cue without a separate exercise or mandatory narrow width.
Both lower and press the same leg-press platform with the back supported. The narrow version changes foot spacing, not the exercise sequence.
Foot placement can remain an optional form preference.
Both are barbell back squats. The candidate prescribes feet 3–6 inches apart rather than a self-selected stable stance.
Personal stance choice; avoid imposing the narrow measurement universally.
Both stand at a low cable and curl while the upper arms stay by the sides. The hammer version uses a rope with palms facing inward instead of the base underhand grip.
Neutral grip changes the forearm position and emphasis; preserve it as an option under the user’s grip-as-preference policy.
Neutral grip instead of palms-up grip

Both current instructions stand with one dumbbell in each hand and curl both together while keeping the upper arms still. Hammer Curl maintains palms inward; Dumbbell Bicep Curl maintains palms forward. Under the stated grip-as-choice policy, this can be one exercise with a grip option.
Neutral grip changes forearm/elbow-flexor emphasis and load tolerance. Retain Hammer Curl as a search alias and grip option rather than erasing the technique choice.
Neutral grip on the same incline curl

Both use a supported incline bench, hanging dumbbells and stationary upper arms for the same bilateral elbow curl. The hammer version keeps the palms inward; the ordinary incline curl turns them forward.
Keep the incline setup and neutral-grip option with its different load tolerance; this is not a proposal to merge incline curls with standing curls.
Both describe consecutive two-foot forward hops over a spaced row of small barriers, rebounding from each landing. The difference is cones versus hurdles; both already allow other small barriers.
Keep cones as a valid equipment alternative and retain per-hop tracking.
Seated Two-Arm Palms-Up Low-Pulley Wrist Curl
Over-specified name for the same setup
Both sit on a bench at a low cable, use a palms-up bar grip, support the forearms on the thighs with wrists beyond the knees, and move only the wrists.
No material movement difference found; preserve old title as a search alias.
Both use a low cable, stationary upper arms by the torso, and elbow flexion followed by a controlled return. The reverse version changes the bar grip from underhand to overhand.
Preserve overhand grip as an option and do not imply identical forearm emphasis or loads.
Both stand and curl a barbell with the upper arms still. The difference is a pronated instead of underhand grip.
Grip changes forearm/biceps emphasis and loading capacity; retain as a documented grip option if consolidated.
Both use an EZ bar with upper arms on a preacher pad and the same elbow flexion/extension. Only the specified grip orientation differs.
Preserve the grip option and its different load tolerance.
Both stand and curl two dumbbells without moving the upper arms. The candidate maintains an overhand grip instead of an underhand grip.
Grip orientation affects emphasis and weight tolerance; preserve as an option.
The candidate is the same standing bilateral dumbbell shoulder press while insisting that the palms stay inward.
Comfortable neutral grip can be offered in the standard press.
Both set the seated handles near the middle chest and press forward by extending the elbows. The leverage version specifies loading plates on pins.
Retain plate-loaded versus selectorized setup cues; the movement can share Machine Chest Press.
Both sit with handles near the shoulders, press upward by extending the elbows, and lower back. The leverage version specifies plate loading.
Simplify the surviving title to Machine Shoulder Press; keep machine-specific seat and loading adjustments.
Both already describe a seated curl machine with upper arms against a pad, forearms flexing at the elbows, then a slow return.
Pad adjustment and stationary upper-arm cues belong in the shared machine curl guidance.
Both start supine with knees bent and feet planted, lift the hips, then lower. The candidate adds a gentle pelvic tilt before the same bridge.
Preserve the tilt cue as optional setup rather than a separate exercise.
Rack bar instead of bench hand support
Both place the hands on a raised support and perform the same straight-body incline push-up. The candidate uses a secured rack bar rather than a stable bench.
Support height, grip and bar security are setup options.
The candidate is a shallow bodyweight squat; the base already asks for a comfortable squat range with grounded feet. No new equipment, sequence, or loading is introduced.
Allow limited comfortable depth as a base form adjustment.
Both lie on a flat bench and lower a bar to the chest before pressing back up. The candidate adds a supinated grip and tucked elbows, rather than a different exercise sequence.
If retained as an option, preserve secure unracking and comfortable wrist/elbow position.
Both lie supine with upper arms perpendicular to the torso and extend only the elbows against a low cable. The variant uses a rope and the seat of a row station instead of a flat bench and bar.
Attachment and stable bench setup; preserve the lying extension position.
Both keep the elbows nearly straight and move at the shoulders to draw a high cable toward the thighs. The distinctive item is the rope.
Rename the surviving display name to Straight-Arm Pulldown and include rope/bar options if approved.
Smith bar used only as hand support
Both hold the body straight with hands on a raised support, lower the chest toward that support, and press away. The Smith bar is not a moving resistance.
A bar must be secured against rotation; support height adjusts difficulty within Incline Push-Up.
Both instructions describe a controlled barbell shrug with straight arms and no leg drive. The candidate changes to a wide snatch grip.
Grip choice and secure bar handling; no ballistic clean/snatch pull is involved.
Both hinge over and row a straight barbell to the torso. The candidate performs the row while standing on a bench, with the bar initially on it.
The elevated setup is unnecessary for the standard row; do not carry bench-standing into default instructions.
Both place a bar across the upper back and hinge at the hips with a steady trunk. The candidate uses softly extended knees instead of the base's slightly bent knees.
A soft knee bend and controlled hip hinge; do not enforce locked knees.
Stiff-legged name for the same authored hinge

The current instructions for both begin standing with the bar near the thighs, keep a soft knee bend, hinge with the bar close and stop before back position changes. The candidate does not describe a floor reset.
Maintain a nearly steady knee angle; this conclusion follows the current catalog instructions, not every possible use of the exercise name.
Both stand at a high cable and extend the elbows with upper arms beside the torso. The base uses a rope while the variant uses a straight bar.
Rename the surviving display name to Cable Triceps Pushdown and include compatible attachment choices if approved.
Both secure the thighs, pull an overhead cable bar toward the upper chest and extend the arms again. The variant prescribes a supinated, closer grip.
Grip orientation and width should be selectable guidance under Lat Pulldown.
Both are seated cable pulldowns toward the upper chest with thighs secured and torso steady. The V-bar version specifies a neutral-grip handle.
Compatible attachment choice and comfortable grip; equipment load histories may differ.
Both press a high cable down by extending the elbows while holding the upper arms still by the torso. The V-bar changes the attachment and hand angle.
Use the same proposed generic Cable Triceps Pushdown base; do not retain an attachment-specific title.
The same rack setup, bar position and squat/stand sequence differ by a wider-than-shoulder-width stance.
Comfortable stance width and knee tracking.
Added band added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the EZ-Bar Curl movement and adds a band to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.
Preserve changing resistance/assistance, anchor setup and load notation as optional modifiers; bar weight alone is not comparable across setups.

Despite its name, the candidate instructions describe a backward lunge plus a torso rotation across the front leg, not a separate crossover step. The base uses the same backward lunge without the twist.
Keep optional torso rotation distinct from the standard base cue; normalize per-side versus total repetition accounting.
Both use overhand pull-ups from a controlled hang. The candidate alternates ordinary pull-ups with a behind-the-head path; no new apparatus or independent movement family is introduced.
Preserve the retired name as an alias if wanted; do not make the special behind-head path part of the default pull-up demonstration.
Angled raise path with thumbs upward

Both stand with two dumbbells at the sides, raise the arms to approximately shoulder height and return. Scaption prescribes an angled forward path and thumbs-forward/up orientation rather than the base lateral path. This fits a broad form-option model but is not instructionally identical.

Preserve the forward-angled plane and thumb orientation. The current wording "30 degrees off center" should be clarified before consolidation; do not silently replace this motion with a strictly sideways raise.
Both squat and jump vertically, absorbing the landing through the legs. Rocket Jump uses a half squat and reaches overhead; the base crosses the arms and describes a deeper squat.
Rename the survivor to Bodyweight Jump Squat if approved, with arm swing and dip depth as options.
Both hinge at the hips with the band around the upper body and then return to standing. The candidate anchors the band to a post; the base stands on the band.
Anchor position changes the resistance direction and requires its own secure setup instructions.
Both shrug a straight-armed barbell by lifting the shoulders. The candidate carries the bar behind the back rather than in front of the thighs.
Behind-body shoulder position and its different setup must remain optional.
Both use a seated pulldown station with thighs secured. The variant routes the bar behind the head rather than to the upper chest.
If retired, keep the ordinary front-of-chest demonstration; do not transfer the behind-neck cue into the standard exercise.
Both use a knee dip and leg drive to push press a barbell overhead without a second receiving dip. The candidate starts across the back rather than front shoulders.
Rear rack setup and comfortable shoulder range are optional; keep strict press and jerk families separate.
Both strictly press a barbell overhead while standing with a braced torso. The candidate starts and returns across the upper back instead of the front shoulders.
Different shoulder range and rack position; do not silently put behind-neck instructions into the default front press.
Both keep the torso supported while bending the knees toward the torso and extending the legs again. The candidate lies on a flat bench with legs beyond its end; the base lies on a mat.
Keep secure bench support and comfortable leg travel as an equipment option.
Chains added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the Barbell Bench Press movement and adds chains to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.
Preserve changing resistance/assistance, anchor setup and load notation as optional modifiers; bar weight alone is not comparable across setups.

The lying T-bar instructions use a chest pad and pull handles toward the torso without lifting off the support, matching the chest-supported Machine Row pattern.
Preserve the chest-supported machine configuration and plate loading. This should not merge into the unsupported landmine T-Bar Row.
Both use one dumbbell and a fixed soft elbow bend through the same overhead pullover arc. The candidate supports only the shoulders across the bench instead of the full back along it.
Foot placement and trunk support are optional setup details.

Both move one dumbbell through an overhead pullover arc. The candidate lies across the bench with hips/head unsupported and calls for straight arms; the base fully supports the back and allows a soft elbow bend.
Optional cross-bench setup; use a soft elbow bend and do not force the unsupported-head position.
Both are seated overhead cable pulls toward the torso. The variant crosses the hands overhead between two towers and rotates the handles during a wider arc.
The dual-cable arc and rotating hands differ from the bar path; retain these as optional setup details, not interchangeable visual references.
Downward bands added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the Box Squat movement and adds downward bands to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.

Downward bands and power-squat style added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the Barbell Squat movement and adds downward bands and power-squat style to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.
Preserve changing resistance/assistance, anchor setup and load notation as optional modifiers; bar weight alone is not comparable across setups.
Both are soft-knee barbell hip hinges from the thighs with a stop before the back changes position. The candidate adds a low stable platform for potential extra range.
Platform height and controlled range; a deficit should not force the bar to the floor.
Both use a Smith bar across the upper back and squat through hip and knee flexion. Despite its name, the chair version has no chair: it chiefly moves the feet about 18 inches forward.
Foot placement changes torso and knee mechanics; keep it as optional coaching rather than silently imposing the same stance.
Both sit with knees bent, lean back slightly, and rotate the trunk gently side to side. The candidate secures the feet; the base simply grounds the heels.
Keep foot anchoring as an optional support choice and retain a consistent per-side repetition convention.
Forearms on thighs instead of bench
Both use two dumbbells and palms down to lift the backs of the hands. The candidate sits with forearms on thighs; the base kneels with forearms on a bench.
Support choice is optional; preserve the same wrist-extension direction.
Forearms on thighs instead of bench
Both use two dumbbells and palms up for supported wrist flexion. The candidate sits with forearms on thighs; the base kneels at the bench.
Support choice is optional; preserve the same palm-up wrist-flexion direction.
Palms-Down Wrist Curl Over A Bench
Forearms supported on bench instead of thighs
Both are overhand barbell wrist extensions with still forearms. The candidate kneels at a bench while the base sits with forearms on the thighs.
Stable support and wrists free to move; preserve reverse wrist extension separately from palm-up flexion.
Palms-Up Barbell Wrist Curl Over A Bench
Forearms supported on bench instead of thighs
Both are underhand barbell wrist curls with still forearms. The candidate kneels at a bench while the base sits with forearms on the thighs.
Choose a stable forearm support; the wrist movement is unchanged despite the whole-body setup.
Both hold a kettlebell overhead and hinge sideways with feet turned away from the loaded side. The advanced version places the free arm behind the back rather than leaving it free for balance/reach.
Extra balance demand is optional; keep the ordinary windmill as the default.
Standing Dumbbell Straight-Arm Front Delt Raise Above Head

Both stand with a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs and raise forward with a steady torso and unchanged soft elbow bend. The candidate continues overhead; the base stops around shoulder height.
Overhead range is a meaningful optional progression and requires controlled shoulder/trunk position; retain the standard shoulder-height default.
Both front-squat with the bar supported on the shoulders. The candidate extends the arms forward without gripping the bar to teach rack position.
It is explicitly a technique drill with a more demanding balance setup; keep that optional drill context.
Barbell Curls Lying Against An Incline
Incline bench instead of preacher-bench chest support
Both are chest-supported straight-bar curls with the arms hanging and elbows held still. The candidate uses an incline bench; Spider Curl uses the chest side of a preacher support.
Support angle and enough bar clearance; both are supported curls, not a standing barbell curl.
Both keep the elbow angle fixed and pull a high cable toward the thighs by moving at the shoulders. The variant lies back on an incline bench rather than standing facing the cable.
Bench angle and orientation change the resistance relationship; retain a supported setup note if consolidated.
Kneeling with head / upper arms supported on bench
Both use a cable to extend the elbows with the upper arms held near the head. The kneeling version adds bench support and a high-pulley bar instead of the standing low-pulley rope.
Bench support, cable direction and arm orientation must remain clear if treated as a setup option.

The candidate holds the legs nearly vertical and reaches the hands toward the toes while curling the torso; the base curls the shoulders with bent knees and grounded feet. The core repetition remains a short trunk curl.
Vertical legs and reaching arms change leverage; keep as an optional crunch setup rather than deleting the cue.
Both use a small rotational crunch bringing one shoulder toward the opposite knee. The candidate crosses one leg over the other on the floor; the base supports the lower legs on a bench.
Broaden the surviving setup to allow floor or supported legs; do not require elbow-to-knee contact.
Both are a small shoulder curl with a steady lower back. The candidate holds the legs bent in tabletop and crosses the ankles instead of planting the feet.
Elevated legs change leverage and support demands; preserve as an optional setup.
Calf Press On The Leg Press Machine
Both are seated, platform-loaded calf presses with knees softly extended and held still while the ankles raise and lower the heels. The longer title specifies a leg-press machine.
Machine-specific safeties and foot-platform security; distinguish from bent-knee Seated Calf Raise.
Both sit at a row machine and pull handles from chest level toward the torso. The iso instructions still use both hands; they do not describe a separate unilateral repetition.
Confirm the specific machine supports the chest, as the generic base assumes; retain plate-loading and handle adjustments.
Both bring two handles together in front of the chest with a steady soft elbow bend. The variant specifies low pulleys and an upward arc from below the waist.
Pulley height and line of pull meaningfully change the emphasis; preserve them as form options if the library uses one crossover entry.
Lying on floor instead of standing
Both keep the elbows by the torso and curl a low-pulley bar with an underhand grip. The floor version changes body support while retaining the same elbow movement.
Body support and cable distance differ; retain a supported setup note rather than using the lying image for standing instructions.
Both sit upright at a low pulley using a rope, keep the upper arms horizontal, and row with elbows flared. One pulls below the neck and the other brings the hands closer to the ears.
Retain the high-elbow rear-delt row cue and a comfortable endpoint; distinct from an elbows-tucked lower-rib cable row.
Both squat with a bar on the upper back. The candidate specifies a high trap position, upright torso, hip-width stance and very deep descent.
High-bar placement and depth can be style cues without requiring every user to adopt them.
Outward curl path and inner-biceps label
Both perform dumbbell curls on an incline bench. The candidate turns the forearms outward and finishes beside the shoulders rather than directly in front.
Different upper-arm/forearm orientation, not a separately isolated inner muscle.
Outward curl path and inner-biceps label
Both stand and curl dumbbells with stationary upper arms. The candidate turns the palms from neutral to upward while curling outward toward the outer deltoids.
Optional curl path and wrist rotation; avoid treating an inner-biceps label as a distinct movement family.
Both sit on a flat bench and curl two dumbbells while rotating from a neutral grip. The candidate directs the forearms outward toward the deltoids.
Keep seated setup as the retained base; outward arm path is the narrower variation.
Overhead assistance bands added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the Barbell Bench Press movement and adds overhead assistance bands to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.
Preserve changing resistance/assistance, anchor setup and load notation as optional modifiers; bar weight alone is not comparable across setups.

Overhead assistance bands and power-squat style added to the standard lift
The candidate retains the Barbell Squat movement and adds overhead assistance bands and power-squat style to the bar or setup. The base supplies the same main movement without that loading accessory.
Preserve changing resistance/assistance, anchor setup and load notation as optional modifiers; bar weight alone is not comparable across setups.
Both perform an anchored-feet sit-up from bent knees. The candidate reverses after only three-quarters of the lowering instead of returning fully.
Partial lowering is a range/tempo option, not a mandatory standard sit-up instruction.
Both lie on an incline bench under a Smith bar and press above the upper chest. The partial version repeats only the short upper portion with slightly bent elbows.
Partial reps are a programming/form option, not evidence that the standard full-range instructions should be shortened.
One-Arm Kettlebell Military Press To The Side
Slightly outward strict kettlebell press path

Both current descriptions clean one bell to the shoulder and strictly press overhead without leg drive or leaning. The candidate starts palm-in and describes a slightly outward path; Para Press starts palm-forward.
Consider simplifying the retained name to Single-Arm Kettlebell Press; preserve the comfortable grip/path option.

Both curl the pelvis backward to lift the hips from the floor. The candidate starts the bent legs only two inches off the floor and draws them farther toward the chest; the base starts with hips and knees near right angles.
Preserve the lower-leg start as a harder optional range, while keeping the controlled pelvic curl central.
Both lean back with grounded heels and straight arms, then row the chest toward the hands. The candidate uses suspension-trainer handles; the base uses rings.
Broaden the surviving name and equipment to Suspension Row if consolidating; keep rated anchors and adjustable body angle.
Tall flat bench instead of preacher-bench support
Both are prone/chest-supported barbell curls with hanging arms and still upper arms. The candidate requires a tall flat bench rather than a preacher support.
Bar clearance and shoulder angle depend on the support.
Both support the body on parallel bars, bend the elbows, and press back up. Chest Dip adds a slight forward lean; Tricep Dip specifies an upright torso.
Rename the survivor to Parallel-Bar Dip and allow controlled torso angle; preserve chest/triceps involvement rather than promising isolation.
Lying Barbell Triceps Extension Behind the Head
Upper arms held behind the head
Both lie on a bench and extend the elbows with upper arms fixed. The candidate holds the upper arms back nearly parallel to the bench instead of pointing above the chest.
This meaningfully changes shoulder position and stretch; preserve it as an optional extension angle.
Both row dumbbells with the chest supported on an incline bench. The candidate flares the elbows into a T while the base rows toward the sides.
Elbow path changes emphasis toward upper back/rear delts; preserve it as an optional cue.
Both hinge and row a barbell. The candidate flares the elbows and pulls toward the upper chest rather than the lower ribs.
Upper-back/rear-delt emphasis and comfortable shoulder range; this is more than a name-only duplicate.

The candidate uses a wide stance and nearly straight legs for repeated barbell hip hinges; after the first lift it need not touch the floor. The retained Romanian Deadlift covers the same repeated hinge pattern with a soft knee bend.
Wide stance and initial floor pickup need explicit optional cues; keep the knees soft.
Both bend and extend the elbows in a hands-behind bench dip. The candidate raises the heels onto a second bench and places a dumbbell on the lap.
External load, assisted loading/unloading, and raised-foot setup must remain explicit and loggable.
Both stand between low cables and press from shoulder height to overhead. One presses each arm in turn while the base presses both together.
Per-side repetition counting and unilateral timing must be preserved if merged.
Alternating arm while other arm holds
Both bring cable handles to the body midline with softly bent elbows. The variant holds one hand forward while moving the other arm and alternates sides.
The stationary-arm hold and per-side repetition convention need an explicit mode; do not silently replace bilateral guidance.
Both are standing dumbbell curls. This version combines a neutral grip with alternating arms instead of curling both together.
Keep neutral grip, arm path and per-side counting as explicit options if merged. The proposal maps directly to Dumbbell Bicep Curl so the survivor is not also scheduled for consolidation.
Both are supinating dumbbell curls while supported on an incline bench. The candidate alternates the arms; the base curls both together.
Optional alternation and consistent repetition convention.
Both raise dumbbells forward from the thighs to approximately shoulder height with a still torso; only the arm order changes.
Offer alternating reps without creating another exercise; preserve the selected counting convention.
Both stand with dumbbells at the shoulders and press without leg drive or trunk lean. The candidate holds one arm at the shoulder while pressing the other.
Alternation is optional; define whether logged reps apply per side.
Both clean two kettlebells from a hanging position to the shoulders. The candidate cleans one at a time while holding the other down.
Alternating timing and per-side count, versus two bells moving together.
Both start two kettlebells at the shoulders and strictly press them overhead. The candidate alternates the arms, keeping the other bell racked.
Per-side count and alternating work/rest; the bilateral base remains distinct from a single-bell press.
Both hinge and row two kettlebells toward the torso. The candidate moves one bell at a time while the other remains down.
Alternating timing and per-side repetition convention.
Both press a kettlebell upward from the floor with the upper arm supported at the bottom. The candidate alternates between two bells while the other arm remains extended.
Second bell is held isometrically overhead; retain that optional setup and per-arm count.
Both clean a barbell and receive it in a front squat. The candidate starts on raised boxes and resets on them rather than lifting from the floor.
Block height and reduced first pull are meaningful technical details.
Both are barbell power cleans received above a full squat. The candidate starts and resets on blocks rather than the floor.
Keep power catch distinct from full clean; preserve block height and start position.
Both receive a snatch in a partial squat above parallel. The candidate starts on blocks instead of the floor.
Block height and shortened first pull; do not collapse power snatch into full snatch.
Both receive the barbell overhead in a squat. The candidate starts and resets on blocks rather than the floor.
Block height and practiced pull segment; keep full-squat catch.
Both lie on a flat bench and press a barbell. The candidate stops the descent on boards placed over the chest, deliberately reducing range.
Range restriction and board height materially affect load comparisons; this is not a simple alias.
Bottoms-Up Clean From The Hang Position
Both clean a single kettlebell from a hang to the shoulder. The candidate balances it inverted above the fist.
